words: ambiguity; inference; explicit; textual evidence; uncertain; competing reading
notes: Cite strong and thorough evidence for what a text says and implies, and name where the text leaves a matter uncertain. Practised on short American stories built on doubt (Hawthorne's 'Young Goodman Brown', Bierce's 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge', Poe's 'The Fall of the House of Usher'; 3,000 to 8,000 words each, 18th and 19th century prose, high qualitative demand from older syntax and allusion) and, for RI, Douglass's Narrative (1845). Change from 9-10: the 11-12 wording adds 'including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain'. Grade 11 takes it this far: the teacher names the open question (was it a dream?), students build the two best readings and the evidence for each, and say what the text never settles. Grade 12 asks students to find the uncertainty themselves in a long text. Limit: an uncertainty is a gap the text leaves, not a reader's lack of knowledge; background is supplied before reading.

words: theme; motif; interact; complex account; objective summary
cross_subject: social-studies:us1-reform-movements (the reform era the novel's Puritan past is read against)
notes: Determine two or more themes in a long text and trace how they develop and build on one another; write an objective summary. Practised on The Scarlet Letter (1850), read whole across about four weeks (about 63,000 words, roughly 1340 Lexile, near the top of the band, dense older syntax), with Hawthorne's 'The Minister's Black Veil' as a short paired read. Change from 9-10: one theme 'shaped and refined by specific details' becomes 'two or more themes ... how they interact and build on one another to produce a complex account'. Grade 11 work: a theme tracker for two themes (private guilt and public punishment; the individual and the community) chapter by chapter, then one paragraph on where they meet (the scaffold scene). Summary stays objective: no judgment, no theme claims inside it. Grade 12 does this on Hamlet without the tracker given.

words: setting; characterization; sequence; author's choice; impact
notes: Analyze the impact of an author's choices about where a story is set, how the action is ordered and how characters are introduced and developed. Practised on American short fiction and one short play: Chopin's 'The Story of an Hour' (about 1,000 words), Gilman's 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (about 6,000 words, diary form), and Glaspell's Trifles (1916, one act). Change from 9-10: RL.9-10.3 asks how complex characters develop and advance the plot; 11-12 widens to the author's choices about all story elements and their impact. Grade 11 work: for each text, one choice (Trifles set in a kitchen; the men offstage), what it does, and what a different choice would lose. Grade 12 applies it to a novel whole (The Great Gatsby). Teacher note: 'The Story of an Hour' and Trifles involve a death and a marriage marked by cruelty, and 'The Yellow Wallpaper' depicts a woman's breakdown under a 'rest cure'; give a short content note and treat the illness as the story frames it, not as diagnosis.

words: connotation; tone; diction; multiple meaning; imagery
notes: Determine figurative and connotative meanings and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning and tone, including words with more than one meaning and language that is fresh or beautiful. Practised on American poems read closely: Dickinson (six to eight poems) and Whitman (sections of 'Song of Myself', 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd'), with Poe's prose for tone. Poems have no usable computed measure; the record rests on meaning, structure and language. Change from 9-10: 'cumulative impact of word choices' becomes 'impact of specific word choices ... including words with multiple meanings or language that is particularly fresh, engaging, or beautiful', and the 11-12 band adds 'Include Shakespeare'. Grade 11 takes the American poets; the Shakespeare part of the code is done in grade 12 (Hamlet). Students choose one word or phrase, give its two meanings in the line, and say what tone the double meaning makes.

words: structure; frame; ending; resolution; aesthetic impact
notes: Analyze how choices about structuring specific parts of a text (where to begin or end, a comedic or tragic resolution) contribute to its overall structure, meaning and aesthetic impact. Practised on short texts where structure is the point: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' (the time jump and the last line), 'The Story of an Hour' (the final sentence), Dickinson's dashes and stanza breaks, and The Scarlet Letter's opening chapter 'The Custom-House' as a frame. Change from 9-10: 'create such effects as mystery, tension, or surprise' becomes 'overall structure and meaning as well as its aesthetic impact'. Grade 11 work: students name one structural choice, its effect on meaning, and its effect on the reader's experience (aesthetic), with evidence. Grade 12 compares a tragic and a comedic resolution across two whole plays.

words: satire; irony; sarcasm; understatement; stated; meant
notes: Analyze a case where grasping point of view means telling what is directly stated from what is really meant (satire, sarcasm, irony, understatement). Practised on short American satire and irony: Twain's 'The War Prayer' (about 1,500 words), Franklin's satirical pieces ('Rules by Which a Great Empire May Be Reduced to a Small One', 1773), and the last line of 'The Story of an Hour'. Change from 9-10: RL.9-10.6 asked for a cultural point of view in world literature; 11-12 moves to the gap between stated and meant. Grade 11 work: a two-column chart (what the speaker says, what the author means) with the clue in the text that signals the gap. Grade 12 takes it to sustained satire (Swift) and dramatic irony in a full play. Teacher note: 'The War Prayer' prays for harm to enemy civilians in order to condemn it; say so before the first read so no student takes the prayer at face value.

words: interpretation; production; staging; performance; source text
notes: Analyze several interpretations of one story, drama or poem (recorded or live productions, recorded readings) and evaluate how each version interprets the source. Practised on Glaspell's Trifles (1916), the band's play by an American dramatist, read in class, then heard or watched in two versions: a public-domain recorded reading and a Curio Class staged reading, or a school or community production where one exists; plus two recorded readings of one Whitman poem. Change from 9-10: RL.9-10.7 compared a subject in two artistic mediums; 11-12 asks students to evaluate several interpretations of the same source text against it. Grade 11 work: for one scene, what each version adds, cuts or stresses, checked line by line against the script. The standard's Shakespeare requirement is met in grade 12 (Hamlet). Teacher note: Trifles turns on a wife who killed an abusive husband; name this before reading.

words: Puritan; Enlightenment; Romanticism; Transcendentalism; realism; period
cross_subject: social-studies:us1-revolution-causes (the colonial and revolutionary setting of the period's texts); social-studies:us1-reform-movements (the reform era of Emerson and Thoreau)
notes: Show knowledge of foundational works of American literature, including how two or more texts from the same period treat a similar theme. Grade 11 takes the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; grade 12 completes the standard with the early twentieth century. Text sets, in the order of the US History I course beside it: revolutionary writing (Franklin, Wheatley's poems), Romantic and Transcendental writing (Emerson, Thoreau, Hawthorne, Poe), and realism (Twain, Chopin, Bierce). Pairs: Emerson's 'Self-Reliance' with Hawthorne's 'Young Goodman Brown' on the individual and doubt; Dickinson with Whitman on the self. Change from 9-10: RL.9-10.9 was how one author transforms a source; 11-12 asks for knowledge of a national literature by period and comparison within a period. Students write how two same-period texts answer one question differently, with evidence from both.

words: stamina; annotation; reread; complexity
notes: Read and comprehend literature and literary nonfiction in the 11-CCR band proficiently, with scaffolding at the high end (the standard's grade 11 statement). Text: 11-CCR band (about 1185 to 1385 Lexile; a drama or poem rests on the qualitative read). Whole long texts this year: The Scarlet Letter (1850) and Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845, about 40,000 words, about 1080 Lexile, placed for its qualitative demand), plus one long book from a Reading Room shelf of American works for independent reading with a log and conference. Change from 9-10: the band rises from 9-10 (about 1050 to 1335) to 11-CCR. Grade 11 keeps supports before, during and after reading (background in under five minutes, a guided first read of hard chapters, a reread for a named purpose); audio sits beside the text, never in place of it. Grade 12 removes the routine supports: by the end of grade 12 reading at the high end is independent.

words: central idea; interact; develop; objective summary; self-reliance; conscience
notes: Determine two or more central ideas of a nonfiction text and analyze how they interact and build on one another; write an objective summary. Practised on the Transcendental essays: Emerson's 'Self-Reliance' (1841, about 10,000 words, read in sections, very high qualitative demand: aphoristic, few transitions) and Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience' (1849, about 9,000 words). Change from 9-10: 'a central idea ... shaped and refined by specific details' becomes 'two or more central ideas ... how they interact and build on one another to provide a complex analysis'. Grade 11 work: the teacher models tracing two ideas in the first section of 'Self-Reliance' (trust yourself; conformity is a cost), students trace them through the rest, then do 'Civil Disobedience' with a partner. Grade 12 does it alone on a twentieth-century essay.

words: sequence; develop; turning point; literacy; interact
cross_subject: social-studies:us1-slavery-resistance (the same narrative read as a primary source in US History I)
notes: Analyze a complex set of ideas or a sequence of events and explain how individuals, ideas or events interact and develop across the text. Practised on Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, read whole (eleven chapters), tracing how the events of his life (learning to read, the fight with Covey, escape) and his ideas about slavery and literacy shape each other. Change from 9-10: 'how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events' becomes 'a complex set of ideas or sequence of events ... how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop'. Grade 11 work: a chapter-by-chapter chart of event, idea it changes, and the line that shows it. Teacher note: the Narrative describes whippings and sexual violence under slavery; read the hardest passages with the class, give a content note first, and keep focus on Douglass's own framing and agency.

words: key term; refine; connotation; technical meaning; liberty
notes: Determine figurative, connotative and technical meanings and analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term over a text. Practised on how Thoreau builds 'conscience' and 'majority' in 'Civil Disobedience', and how Douglass uses 'freedom' and 'Christianity' (including the Appendix that separates two meanings). Change from 9-10: 'cumulative impact of word choices on meaning and tone' becomes 'how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text'. Grade 11 work: a term log (each use, the page, what it adds or excludes). Grade 12 takes it to legal and political texts, Madison's 'faction' being the standard's own example.

words: structure; premise; grievance; evaluate; effectiveness
notes: Analyze and evaluate whether the structure of an argument or exposition makes its points clear, convincing and engaging. Practised on the Declaration of Independence (about 1,300 words: premise, grievances, conclusion) and Paine's The American Crisis No. 1 (1776, about 4,000 words). Change from 9-10: 'how ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions' becomes 'analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure', so students judge, not only describe. Grade 11 work: map the structure, then argue whether one choice (the long list of grievances) helps or weakens the case for its first audience. Grade 12 evaluates longer, less familiar structures (court opinions, a modern essay).

words: rhetoric; style; stance; premise; tone; emphasis
notes: Determine an author's point of view or purpose where the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content give the text its power; for SL, evaluate a speaker's stance, premises, word choice, emphasis and tone. Practised on Douglass's 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (1852, about 10,000 words, read in parts and heard in a recorded public-domain reading) and Sojourner Truth's 1851 remarks in two transcriptions. Change from 9-10: 'how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view' becomes how 'style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness, or beauty'; SL.11-12.3 adds 'stance, premises, links among ideas, word choice, points of emphasis, and tone'. Grade 11 work: mark three moves in one passage and say what each does to the 1852 audience. Grade 12 owns both codes on twentieth-century addresses heard as recordings.

words: integrate; format; data; photograph; credibility; discrepancy
cross_subject: social-studies:us1-immigration (tenement life and immigration in the industrial city); math:S-ID.B.5 (reading a two-way table of census data)
notes: Integrate and evaluate sources in different formats (words, images, numbers) to address a question; for SL, judge each source's credibility and note discrepancies among the data. Practised on Riis's How the Other Half Lives (1890, chapters) with his photographs, an 1890s census table on the same wards, and a letter of the time; the question: what did tenement life look like, and how far can Riis's account be trusted? Change from 9-10: RI.9-10.7 compared accounts in different mediums; 11-12 asks to integrate them 'to address a question or solve a problem'; SL.11-12.2 adds 'noting any discrepancies among the data'. Grade 11 uses a set the teacher gives. Teacher note: Riis describes immigrant groups in the ethnic stereotypes of his day; read those lines as evidence of his view and say so before reading.

words: premise; purpose; reasoning; public advocacy; delineate
cross_subject: social-studies:us1-revolution-causes (the arguments for independence in their setting)
notes: Delineate and evaluate the premises, purposes and arguments in works of public advocacy. Grade 11 starts the standard on revolutionary advocacy: Paine's Common Sense (1776, selected sections, about 6,000 words) and the Declaration's argument, mapping premise, reasons and the conclusion they claim. Change from 9-10: RI.9-10.8 asked whether reasoning is valid and evidence relevant and sufficient, and to find fallacies; 11-12 names 'seminal U.S. texts', legal reasoning and constitutional principles. Grade 11 takes the advocacy part only; the legal part (Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents) and The Federalist are done in grade 12, beside the government course.

words: covenant; consent; preamble; amendment; inaugural; theme
cross_subject: social-studies:us1-declaration (the Declaration read as an argument in US History I); social-studies:us1-articles-constitution (the Constitution and Bill of Rights in their making)
notes: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth- and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents for their themes, purposes and rhetorical features. Grade 11 reads the core set in order, short and whole: the Mayflower Compact (1620), Winthrop's 'A Model of Christian Charity' (1630, the 'city upon a hill' passage), the Declaration of Independence, the Preamble, the Bill of Rights, and Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address (1865, about 700 words). Change from 9-10: RI.9-10.9 read seminal documents for related themes; 11-12 adds the three centuries, 'purposes, and rhetorical features'. Grade 11 work: for each, its purpose, its audience and one rhetorical feature (the Second Inaugural's balanced clauses). Grade 12 owns it, adding documents that answer these ones.

words: claim; counterclaim; significance; concession; rebuttal; audience
notes: Write arguments on substantive texts and topics with valid reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence (W.11-12.1a to e), drawing evidence from the texts read (W.11-12.9a literature, 9b nonfiction). Two process pieces: a literary argument on The Scarlet Letter (about 1,200 words) and an argument on whether Thoreau's case for civil disobedience holds (about 1,000 words, with two other sources). Change from 9-10: 11-12 adds 'establish the significance of the claim(s)', counterclaims developed 'in a manner that anticipates the audience's knowledge level, concerns, values, and possible biases', and 'varied syntax' for cohesion. Grade 11 work: a model essay from the course, an argument map before drafting, and a named counterclaim paragraph. The rubric is the argument rubric used all year. Writing share by grade 12: about 40 argument, 40 informative, 20 narrative (the standards' own distribution).

words: explain; synthesis; extended definition; analogy; cohesion
notes: Write informative and explanatory texts that convey complex ideas through effective selection, organization and analysis (W.11-12.2a to f). One process piece (about 1,200 words): an explanatory essay defining Transcendentalism for a reader who has never met it, built from Emerson, Thoreau and one later essay, with an extended definition and at least one analogy; plus short on-demand explanations. Change from 9-10: 11-12 asks that 'each new element builds on that which precedes it to create a unified whole', adds 'metaphor, simile, and analogy to manage the complexity of the topic', and asks for implications or significance in the conclusion. Grade 11 work: plan the order so each section depends on the one before, and check it by a partner reading only the topic sentences.

words: point of view; plot line; pacing; reflection; telling detail
notes: Write narratives using effective technique, telling detail and well-structured sequences (W.11-12.3a to e). One process piece (about 1,500 words): a story that tells one event from two points of view, on the model of Trifles (what the men see, what the women see), or a story set in a period read this year. Change from 9-10: 11-12 adds 'setting out a problem, situation, or observation and its significance', 'multiple plot lines', and building toward 'a particular tone and outcome (e.g., ... growth, or resolution)'. Grade 11 takes the two-line structure; grade 12 writes a reflective personal narrative where the significance is the writer's own.

words: revise; feedback; audience; purpose; publish; update
notes: Produce clear, coherent writing fitted to task, purpose and audience; strengthen it by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach; use technology to publish and update it in response to feedback. Practised on each of the year's process pieces, with one named feedback step each (peer read on one look-for, teacher conference). Change from 9-10: W.11-12.6 replaces 'taking advantage of technology's capacity to link' with 'update ... in response to ongoing feedback, including new arguments or information'; editing for conventions is held to L.11-12.1 to 3. Grade 11 work: students publish the Thoreau argument to a shared class page and revise it once after reading a classmate's opposing piece. The plan says what a room without devices does (a paper draft and a posted revision).

words: research question; narrow; broaden; authoritative; limitation; plagiarism
cross_subject: social-studies:us1-research-inquiry (the same research cycle in US History I)
notes: Conduct short and more sustained research to answer a question; gather from authoritative print and digital sources with advanced searches, assess each source's strengths and limitations, integrate selectively, avoid plagiarism and overreliance on one source, and cite in a standard format. Two projects: a short one (three days, three sources) on the context of an American text, and a four-week project on a nineteenth-century reform movement (abolition, women's rights, temperance) with at least five sources, ending in an essay of about 1,500 words and a talk. Change from 9-10: W.11-12.8 replaces 'assess the usefulness of each source' with 'assess the strengths and limitations of each source in terms of the task, purpose, and audience' and adds 'overreliance on any one source'. Grade 11 gives the topic area; the question is the student's. Grade 12 runs a longer, self-generated project.

words: on-demand; analysis; reflection; draw evidence
notes: Write routinely over extended time frames and short ones (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks and audiences. Practised daily: the exit question on the day's text, a weekly one-sitting analytic paragraph, and three one-sitting essays a year on a cold passage (one per writing type). Change from 9-10: the wording is the same across the two bands; the rise is in the texts written about and the 11-12 demands of W.1 to W.3. No timer is shown to students; the teacher keeps time.

words: seminar; probe; civil; synthesize; divergent; position
notes: Initiate and take part in collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, teacher-led) on grade 11 texts and issues, building on others' ideas (SL.11-12.1a to d). Practised in a seminar each unit: on 'Self-Reliance' and 'Civil Disobedience', on the Douglass speech, on Trifles. Change from 9-10: 11-12 adds 'promote civil, democratic discussions and decision-making', 'ensure a hearing for a full range of positions', and 'resolve contradictions when possible' and decide what further research is needed. Grade 11 work: students prepare with marked evidence, take named roles that rotate (opener, prober, synthesizer), and end each seminar with a written synthesis of two positions. Grade 12 runs seminars student-led, setting their own goals and deadlines.

words: perspective; line of reasoning; opposing view; formal register
notes: Present findings with a clear and distinct perspective, so listeners follow the reasoning, with opposing perspectives addressed; use digital media strategically; adapt speech to context, with formal English when fitting. Practised on the reform-movement research talk (about six minutes, with slides or a handout) and one informal talk (a short reading-aloud with an introduction). Change from 9-10: SL.11-12.4 adds 'conveying a clear and distinct perspective' and 'alternative or opposing perspectives are addressed' and 'a range of formal and informal tasks'. Grade 11 work: a model talk, a planning sheet with the opposing view slot, and feedback on one look-for. Grade 12 presents the senior research and adapts one talk to two audiences.

words: convention; usage; contested; hyphenation; usage guide
notes: Command of standard grammar, usage, capitalization, punctuation and spelling, with the understanding that usage is a matter of convention, changes over time and is sometimes contested (L.11-12.1a), resolving hard cases with a usage guide (1b), hyphenation (2a) and spelling (2b). Practised on American texts that show usage changing: Webster's spelling reforms, Franklin's capitals, Dickinson's dashes, Twain's dialect; and on students' own drafts during editing. Change from 9-10: 9-10 asked for parallel structure, phrases and clauses, and semicolons and colons; 11-12 turns to usage as convention and to hyphenation. Grade 11 work: contrast an eighteenth-century and a modern edition of one passage and say what changed; edit drafts for hyphenated compound modifiers. The progressive skills to grade 10 (including parallel structure) are kept in editing.

words: syntax; periodic sentence; parallelism; catalog; effect
notes: Apply knowledge of how language functions to make choices for meaning or style; vary syntax for effect and use an understanding of syntax to read complex texts (L.11-12.3a). Practised on sentences from the year's anchors: Hawthorne's periodic sentences, Whitman's catalogs, Lincoln's balanced clauses, Douglass's antithesis. Change from 9-10: L.9-10.3a asked for writing to a style manual; 11-12 asks to 'vary syntax for effect' and to read complex texts through their syntax. Grade 11 work: unpack one long anchor sentence into its parts, recombine it two ways, and say what each version stresses; then revise a paragraph of one's own draft. Sentence combining is the named method.

words: etymology; archaic; derivation; part of speech; verify
notes: Determine or clarify unknown and multiple-meaning words from grade 11 reading, choosing flexibly among context, word changes (conceive, conception, conceivable), reference works for etymology and usage, and checking a first guess. Practised on the archaic and shifted words of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century texts ('awful', 'presently', 'want', 'nice'), where context alone misleads. Change from 9-10: the wording is nearly the same; the rise is the older texts and the step of verifying an inferred meaning (4d). Grade 11 work: a guess from context, a check in a historical dictionary entry, and a note on how the meaning has moved.

words: paradox; hyperbole; denotation; connotation; nuance
notes: Interpret figures of speech such as hyperbole and paradox in context and analyze their role (L.11-12.5a); analyze nuances in words with similar denotations (5b). Practised on Thoreau's and Emerson's paradoxes ('the government is best which governs not at all'), Dickinson's slant figures, and pairs of near-synonyms from the anchors (liberty and freedom; slave and enslaved as used then and now). Change from 9-10: 9-10 named euphemism and oxymoron; 11-12 names hyperbole and paradox and asks for their role in the text. Grade 11 work: for one paradox, say what is contradictory, what truth it holds, and why the author chose the contradiction.

words: general academic word; domain word; word list
notes: Acquire and use general academic and domain words at the college and career level, gathering vocabulary on one's own. Practised on each unit's word list, drawn from its texts (about 15 words a unit, mostly general academic: 'sovereign', 'conscience', 'compulsory', 'prejudice'), met before, during and after reading and back in later units. Change from 9-10: the wording is the same; the rise is in the words of the 11-CCR texts and in students keeping their own list. Grade 11 work: students add three words a unit to their own log from independent reading, with sentence and source.

words: ambiguity; equivocation; inference; textual evidence; uncertain
notes: Owns RL.11-12.1 and RI.11-12.1: cite strong and thorough evidence for what a text says and implies, including where it leaves matters uncertain. Practised on Hamlet (is the Ghost honest? is the madness feigned?) and on court opinions (what the majority leaves open). Change from grade 11: the wording is the same across the band; grade 11 named the open question, grade 12 students find the uncertainty themselves in a long text and argue what follows from it, with evidence from more than one place in the text. RL gives the literary part, RI the nonfiction and legal part.

words: theme; interact; complex account; objective summary; revenge
notes: Owns RL.11-12.2: two or more themes, how they interact and build to a complex account, and an objective summary. Practised on Hamlet, read whole across about five weeks (the play has no usable computed measure; the record rests on Early Modern English, its length and its ambiguity, the hardest literary text in the course). Themes traced: revenge and justice, action and delay, appearance and truth, mortality. Change from grade 11: the same standard, now on a full play without the theme tracker given; students choose the themes and show where they meet (the graveyard scene). Teacher note: the play includes suicide (Ophelia, the 'To be, or not to be' soliloquy); give a content note, discuss as the play frames it, and give the school's support contacts.

words: narrator; frame; setting; sequence; characterization
notes: Owns RL.11-12.3: the impact of an author's choices about setting, the order of action and how characters are introduced and developed. Practised on The Great Gatsby (1925), read whole (about 48,000 words, about 1070 Lexile but high qualitative demand: unreliable narration, nonlinear order, symbol), with Nick as narrator, the delayed entrance of Gatsby, and the settings of East and West Egg and the valley of ashes. Change from grade 11: grade 11 did short stories and a one-act play; grade 12 traces the choices across a whole novel and argues their combined effect. Teacher note: the novel includes Tom's racist talk, a fatal car crash and a killing; read the racist lines as Fitzgerald's portrait of Tom.

words: pun; connotation; tone; diction; soliloquy
notes: Owns RL.11-12.4: figurative and connotative meanings, the impact of word choice on meaning and tone, words with multiple meanings, and language that is fresh or beautiful, including Shakespeare. Practised on Hamlet's soliloquies and puns ('a little more than kin, and less than kind') and on early twentieth-century poems (Eliot's 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock', Hughes, McKay, Frost). Change from grade 11: grade 11 did American poets; grade 12 completes the code with Shakespeare's language, where a word's Early Modern meaning must be checked before its effect can be argued.

words: tragic resolution; comedic resolution; structure; aesthetic impact
notes: Owns RL.11-12.5: how choices about structuring specific parts of a text (where to begin or end, a comedic or tragic resolution) contribute to its overall structure, meaning and aesthetic impact. Practised on two whole plays set side by side: Hamlet's tragic ending and Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (1895, three acts, comic resolution through a found handbag), and on Gatsby's opening and closing pages. Change from grade 11: grade 11 analyzed single structural choices in short texts; grade 12 compares how two whole works use resolution, which is the standard's own example pair.

words: satire; verbal irony; dramatic irony; understatement; persona
notes: Owns RL.11-12.6: point of view that depends on telling stated from meant (satire, sarcasm, irony, understatement). Practised on Swift's 'A Modest Proposal' (1729, about 3,400 words, sustained satire with a persona), the opening chapters of Austen's Pride and Prejudice (irony in the narrator), the wit of Earnest, and Hamlet's sarcasm and dramatic irony. Change from grade 11: grade 11 read short satire with the gap flagged; grade 12 reads sustained satire where the persona never breaks, and students must prove the author's real view from the text alone. Teacher note: 'A Modest Proposal' proposes eating poor children to condemn the treatment of the Irish poor; set up satire and the Irish famine context before the first read.

words: production; interpretation; staging; director; evaluate
notes: Owns RL.11-12.7: analyze several interpretations of a story, drama or poem and evaluate how each interprets the source, including at least one play by Shakespeare and one by an American dramatist. Practised on Hamlet: two or three versions of the same scenes (the closet scene, 'To be, or not to be'): a public-domain recording (an early film or a full-cast audio reading), a Curio Class staged reading, and a live school or community production where one exists. Change from grade 11: the American dramatist part was met in grade 11 with Trifles; grade 12 adds Shakespeare and asks students to judge which version is truest to the text and why, with lines as evidence.

words: modernism; Harlem Renaissance; Jazz Age; American dream; period
cross_subject: social-studies:us2-twenties-culture (the 1920s and the Harlem Renaissance in US History II)
notes: Owns RL.11-12.9: knowledge of foundational American literature of the eighteenth, nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, including how two texts of one period treat a similar theme. Grade 11 covered the first two centuries; grade 12 completes the span with the early twentieth: The Great Gatsby with Harlem Renaissance poems (Hughes's 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', McKay's 'If We Must Die', Cullen) and Toomer's Cane (1923, excerpts), on the American dream and who it includes. Change from grade 11: grade 11 compared within a period with pairs given; grade 12 students choose the pair and also look back, setting one 1920s text against a nineteenth-century one on the same theme. Teacher note: 'If We Must Die' answers the racial violence of 1919; give the historical setting before reading.

words: independent; stamina; complexity; annotation
notes: Owns RL.11-12.10 and RI.11-12.10: by the end of grade 12, read literature and literary nonfiction at the high end of the 11-CCR band independently and proficiently. Text: 11-CCR band (about 1185 to 1385 Lexile; drama and poetry by the qualitative read). Whole long texts: Hamlet and The Great Gatsby, plus one long independent book (Frankenstein, 1818, offered first), with log and conference. Change from grade 11: grade 11 read 'with scaffolding as needed'; grade 12 removes the routine supports across the year, so by the last unit students read a new text cold and alone. The end-of-unit assessment texts are cold reads at the high end of the band.

words: central idea; interact; complex analysis; objective summary
notes: Owns RI.11-12.2: two or more central ideas, how they interact and build to a complex analysis, with an objective summary. Practised on Woolf's A Room of One's Own (1929, chapters 1 and 3, about 15,000 words, high qualitative demand from a wandering structure and an invented narrator) and Du Bois's 'Of Our Spiritual Strivings' (1903). Change from grade 11: grade 11 traced two ideas the teacher named, with modelling; grade 12 students find and trace them alone, and the summary must hold a text whose structure does not signal its ideas.

words: double consciousness; develop; interact; sequence
notes: Owns RI.11-12.3: analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and how individuals, ideas or events interact and develop. Practised on Du Bois's The Souls of Black Folk (1903, chapters 1 to 3), tracing how his idea of double consciousness meets the history he narrates (Reconstruction, the Freedmen's Bureau) and his answer to Booker T. Washington. Change from grade 11: grade 11 traced a single life narrative; grade 12 traces ideas and events woven through an argued history, where the order is the author's argument.

words: key term; faction; technical meaning; refine; define
cross_subject: social-studies:gov-founding-documents (The Federalist in the government course)
notes: Owns RI.11-12.4: figurative, connotative and technical meanings, and how an author uses and refines a key term over a text. Practised on Madison's 'faction' in Federalist No. 10 (1787, about 3,000 words, the standard's own example), Du Bois's 'the veil', and technical legal terms in court opinions ('equal protection', 'due process'). Change from grade 11: grade 11 tracked a key term in essays; grade 12 adds technical and legal meanings, where a defined term carries the argument.

words: holding; majority; dissent; structure; effectiveness
notes: Owns RI.11-12.5: analyze and evaluate whether the structure of an exposition or argument makes its points clear, convincing and engaging. Practised on the structure of a court opinion (facts, question, holding, reasoning, dissent) in Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) and on Woolf's essay, whose looping structure students judge for and against. Change from grade 11: grade 11 evaluated familiar argument structures; grade 12 evaluates unfamiliar and long ones, including a structure that is effective for one audience and not another.

words: rhetoric; style; stance; premise; emphasis; tone
notes: Owns RI.11-12.6 and SL.11-12.3: an author's point of view or purpose where the rhetoric is particularly effective, how style and content give a text its power or beauty; for SL, evaluating a speaker's stance, premises, links among ideas, word choice, emphasis and tone. Practised on twentieth-century presidential addresses read and heard as public-domain recordings (Franklin Roosevelt's First Inaugural, 1933; Kennedy's Inaugural, 1961) and one current public speech chosen by the teacher. Change from grade 11: grade 11 read nineteenth-century speeches in print with a recorded reading; grade 12 listens to the speaker's own delivery and judges how delivery (pause, emphasis) adds to the words.

words: integrate; data; discrepancy; credibility; decision
cross_subject: math:S-IC.B.6 (evaluating reports based on data); social-studies:gov-policy-debates (a current policy question in the government course)
notes: Owns RI.11-12.7 and SL.11-12.2: integrate and evaluate sources in different media and formats (visual, quantitative, oral, words) to address a question or make a decision, judging each source's credibility and noting discrepancies among the data. Practised on a current public question (for example, a city's choice about housing or transit) with a government data table, a chart, a news report, an op-ed and a recorded public hearing. Change from grade 11: grade 11 integrated a historical set given by the teacher; grade 12 students build part of the set, use it to reach a decision, and name what the sources disagree on.

words: majority opinion; dissent; precedent; constitutional principle; legal reasoning
cross_subject: social-studies:gov-courts (the Supreme Court and judicial review in the government course); social-studies:gov-rights-cases (rights cases read for their holdings)
notes: Owns RI.11-12.8: delineate and evaluate reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including constitutional principles and legal reasoning in Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents, and the premises and arguments of public advocacy. Practised on Federalist No. 10 and No. 51, Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) with Harlan's dissent, Brown v. Board of Education (1954), and Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) with Black's dissent (opinions in excerpt, 2,000 to 4,000 words each). Change from grade 11: grade 11 mapped revolutionary advocacy; grade 12 adds legal reasoning (precedent, the principle applied, the test the court sets) and judges majority against dissent. Teacher note: the Plessy majority reasons from racial segregation; read it as the law it was, beside Harlan's dissent and Brown.

words: declaration; sentiments; theme; purpose; rhetorical feature
cross_subject: social-studies:gov-founding-documents (the founding documents in the government course); social-studies:gov-ideals-gap (the ideals and the gaps in practice)
notes: Owns RI.11-12.9: analyze seventeenth- to nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents for themes, purposes and rhetorical features. Grade 11 read the core set; grade 12 reads documents that answer it and compares across the set: the Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments (1848) against the Declaration of Independence, the Fourteenth Amendment against the Bill of Rights, and Lincoln's Second Inaugural against the Gettysburg Address. Change from grade 11: grade 11 analyzed each document alone; grade 12 analyzes how a later document reuses an earlier one's words for a new purpose, and does one new document cold.

words: claim; counterclaim; bias; significance; formal style
notes: Owns W.11-12.1 (a to e): arguments on substantive topics or texts with valid reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence. Two process pieces: a literary argument on Hamlet (about 1,500 words) and a constitutional argument written as a mock opinion or dissent on a case the class has not read the ruling of (about 1,200 words). Change from grade 11: grade 11 named one counterclaim; grade 12 develops claims and counterclaims 'fairly and thoroughly', pointing out the strengths and limitations of both for a named audience, and keeps a formal style 'attending to the norms and conventions of the discipline' (literary criticism; legal writing).

words: explain; complex concept; analogy; graphic; implication
cross_subject: social-studies:econ-fiscal-monetary (an economic idea explained for a general reader)
notes: Owns W.11-12.2 (a to f): informative and explanatory texts on complex ideas, with headings, graphics and multimedia where they help. One process piece (about 1,500 words): explain a complex idea from another course (an economic policy, a scientific concept) to a general reader, with a figure or table and an analogy, and end on its implications. Change from grade 11: grade 11 explained a literary movement from texts read; grade 12 explains a concept from outside ELA, chooses its own sources, and must manage technical vocabulary for a reader without it.

words: reflection; significance; telling detail; pacing
notes: Owns W.11-12.3 (a to e): narratives of real or imagined experience using effective technique, telling detail and structured sequences. One process piece: a reflective personal narrative (about 650 to 1,000 words, the length of an application essay) that sets out an experience and its significance and ends on what was learned or changed; one short story choice for students who prefer fiction. Change from grade 11: grade 11 wrote a two-point-of-view story; grade 12 adds reflection as a technique and a conclusion that 'reflects on what is experienced', with the writer's own significance at the centre. Teacher note: personal narratives can surface private matters; students choose what to share and nothing is read aloud without consent.

words: revise; rewrite; new approach; publish; update; feedback
notes: Owns W.11-12.4, W.11-12.5 and W.11-12.6: writing fitted to task, purpose and audience; strengthened by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or a new approach, focused on what matters most for purpose and audience; published and updated with technology in response to ongoing feedback. Practised on every grade 12 process piece. Change from grade 11: grade 11 revised once after one feedback step; grade 12 students plan their own revision from the rubric, try at least one new approach on one piece (a different structure or opening), and keep an updated portfolio that carries their best argument, informative and narrative pieces.

words: self-generated question; synthesize; authoritative; limitation; annotated bibliography
cross_subject: social-studies:us2-research-paper (the research paper in US History II)
notes: Owns W.11-12.7 and W.11-12.8: short and sustained research to answer a question, including a self-generated one, narrowing or broadening the inquiry, synthesizing sources; gathering from authoritative sources with advanced searches, judging each source's strengths and limitations, integrating selectively, avoiding plagiarism and overreliance on one source, citing in a standard format. The senior research project (about eight weeks): the student's own question, at least eight sources with an annotated list, an essay of about 2,500 words, and a talk. Change from grade 11: grade 11 gave the topic area; grade 12 the question is self-generated and the student documents one narrowing or broadening of the inquiry and why.

words: analysis; reflection; evidence; on-demand
notes: Owns W.11-12.9 (draw evidence from literary and informational texts for analysis, reflection and research; 9a applies the 11-12 reading standards to literature, 9b to literary nonfiction) and W.11-12.10 (write routinely over long and short time frames). Practised daily in the exit question and weekly in a one-sitting analytic paragraph; three one-sitting essays on cold texts across the year. Change from grade 11: the same standards; grade 12 one-sitting essays draw on two texts at once (a literary text and an informational one), applying 9a and 9b together. No timer is shown to students.

words: seminar; probe; synthesize; contradiction; consensus
notes: Owns SL.11-12.1 (a to d): collaborative discussion on grade 12 texts and issues, prepared with evidence, civil and democratic, posing and answering questions that probe reasoning, hearing a full range of positions, synthesizing and resolving contradictions. Practised in seminars on Hamlet, the court cases and the policy question. Change from grade 11: grade 11 seminars had rotating roles set by the teacher; grade 12 seminars are student-led: the group sets its goal and deadline, assigns roles, and ends by naming what further research would settle a disagreement (SL.11-12.1d).

words: perspective; reasoning; digital media; register; audience
notes: Owns SL.11-12.4, SL.11-12.5 and SL.11-12.6: present findings with a clear, distinct perspective and opposing views addressed, organization and style fitted to purpose, audience and formal or informal tasks; use digital media strategically; adapt speech to context. Practised on the senior research talk (about ten minutes with questions, with visuals chosen to show evidence) and one talk given twice to two audiences (a panel of adults, then younger students). Change from grade 11: grade 11 gave one formal talk with a planning sheet; grade 12 adapts the same content to two contexts and answers live questions.

words: contested usage; convention; usage guide; hyphenation
notes: Owns L.11-12.1 (1a usage as convention that changes and is contested; 1b resolving complex or contested usage with references) and L.11-12.2 (2a hyphenation; 2b spelling). Practised on contested cases students meet in their own writing (singular 'they', 'data is' or 'are', split infinitives, 'who' or 'whom'), each settled for a named audience with a usage guide, and on editing the senior research paper. Change from grade 11: grade 11 saw usage change in older texts; grade 12 students make and defend usage choices in their own formal writing for a discipline's norms.

words: syntax; parallelism; inversion; fragment for effect; style
notes: Owns L.11-12.3 (and 3a): apply knowledge of language to make choices for meaning or style, vary syntax for effect, and read complex texts through their syntax. Practised on Shakespeare's inverted syntax, Fitzgerald's long cumulative sentences, Woolf's sentences, and the student's own drafts. Change from grade 11: grade 11 recombined anchor sentences; grade 12 students revise a whole paragraph of their own for one effect and explain each change, and read Early Modern English syntax for sense.

words: etymology; Early Modern English; derivation; verify
notes: Owns L.11-12.4 (4a to 4d): determine or clarify unknown and multiple-meaning words, choosing flexibly from context, word changes, references and verification. Practised on Hamlet's Early Modern vocabulary ('quietus', 'bodkin', 'rank', 'conscience' in its older sense of knowledge) and the technical words of court opinions. Change from grade 11: the same standard; grade 12 applies it to Shakespeare and legal language, where a word's older or technical meaning changes the reading of a whole passage.

words: paradox; hyperbole; nuance; denotation; connotation
notes: Owns L.11-12.5 (5a figures of speech such as hyperbole and paradox in context and their role; 5b nuances of words with similar denotations). Practised on Hamlet's paradoxes ('I must be cruel only to be kind'), Wilde's epigrams in Earnest, and near-synonyms in court opinions and addresses. Change from grade 11: grade 11 interpreted paradox in essays and poems; grade 12 analyzes figures whose role is dramatic or comic and judges word choice where near-synonyms carry legal weight.

words: general academic word; domain word; independence
notes: Owns L.11-12.6: acquire and use general academic and domain words at the college and career level, with independence in gathering vocabulary. Practised on unit word lists from the texts (about 15 a unit) and, above all, on the student's own list from the senior research and independent reading. Change from grade 11: grade 11 added three words a unit to a teacher list; grade 12 students build the research project's word list themselves and use it in the paper and talk.
